title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text: What will our sales look like for the next quarter? Accurate short-horizon sales forecasts drive staffing, stock, and cash-flow decisions. I build a simple but honest forecast pipeline on two years of synthetic daily sales.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text: What will our sales look like for the next quarter? Accurate short-horizon sales forecasts drive staffing, stock, and cash-flow decisions. I build a simple but honest forecast pipeline on two years of synthetic daily sales.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
The Approach

Generate a realistic-looking sales series (trend + weekly seasonality + noise)
Decompose it into components so we understand what is moving
Forecast the next 90 days with moving-average smoothing
Build an interactive dashboard to explore the forecast

The centred \(n\)-period moving average used for trend extraction is:1
\[\hat{T}_t = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=-(n-1)/2}^{(n-1)/2} y_{t+i}\]
where \(y_t\) is the observed sales value at time \(t\) and \(n = 30\) days is the window chosen to smooth out weekly seasonality without over-smoothing the trend.





flowchart LR
    A[Raw Daily Sales] --> B[Decomposition]
    B --> C[Trend]
    B --> D[Weekly Seasonality]
    B --> E[Residual]
    C --> F[Forecast Engine]
    D --> F
    F --> G[90-Day Forecast]
    F --> H[80% Confidence Band]
    G --> I[Interactive Dashboard]
    H --> I

    style I fill:#8ac926,color:#fff

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Step 1 — Simulate daily sales


Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(7)

# 730 days ending today
dates = pd.date_range(end='2026-04-15', periods=730)

# Trend: slow upward growth
trend = np.linspace(1000, 1800, 730)

# Weekly seasonality: weekends ~30% higher
day_of_week = dates.dayofweek
weekly = np.where(day_of_week >= 5, 300, 0) + np.sin(day_of_week * np.pi / 3.5) * 80

# Yearly seasonality: December spike
month = dates.month
yearly = np.where(month == 12, 400, 0) + np.where(month.isin([6, 7]), 150, 0)

# Noise
noise = np.random.normal(0, 60, 730)

sales = (trend + weekly + yearly + noise).round(2)

df = pd.DataFrame({'Date': dates, 'Sales': sales})

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
section: Step 3 — Decompose into trend, season, residual
text:
Step 3 — Decompose into trend, season, residual


Code
# Simple moving averages to extract components
df['Trend'] = df['Sales'].rolling(window=30, center=True).mean()
df['Detrended'] = df['Sales'] - df['Trend']
df['Seasonal'] = df.groupby(df['Date'].dt.dayofweek)['Detrended'].transform('mean')
df['Residual'] = df['Sales'] - df['Trend'] - df['Seasonal']

fig = make_subplots(rows=3, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                     subplot_titles=('Trend (30-day moving average)', 'Weekly seasonality', 'Residual'))

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=df['Date'], y=df['Trend'], line=dict(color='#6a4c93'), name='Trend'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=df['Date'], y=df['Seasonal'], line=dict(color='#1982c4'), name='Season'), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=df['Date'], y=df['Residual'], line=dict(color='#ff595e'), name='Residual'), row=3, col=1)

fig.update_layout(height=600, showlegend=False, template='plotly_white')
fig.show()




                                                


Figure 2: Classical decomposition of the sales series




The decomposition confirms the trend is genuinely increasing (business growing), the weekly seasonality is stable (reliable to forecast), and the residual is well-behaved (no missed pattern).

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Step 4 — Forecast the next 90 days


Code
# A simple but honest forecast: trend projection + average seasonality
future_dates = pd.date_range(start=df['Date'].max() + pd.Timedelta(days=1), periods=90)

# Extend the trend linearly from last known trend value
last_trend = df['Trend'].dropna().iloc[-15:].mean()
trend_slope = (df['Trend'].dropna().iloc[-15:].mean() - df['Trend'].dropna().iloc[-45:-30].mean()) / 30
future_trend = last_trend + trend_slope * np.arange(1, 91)

# Apply the weekly seasonality map
dow_seasonality = df.groupby(df['Date'].dt.dayofweek)['Seasonal'].mean()
future_seasonal = future_dates.to_series().dt.dayofweek.map(dow_seasonality).values

forecast = future_trend + future_seasonal

# 80% confidence interval from residual std
residual_std = df['Residual'].std()
upper = forecast + 1.28 * residual_std
lower = forecast - 1.28 * residual_std

forecast_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Date': future_dates,
    'Forecast': forecast.round(2),
    'Upper': upper.round(2),
    'Lower': lower.round(2)
})

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=df['Date'], y=df['Sales'], name='Historical',
                          line=dict(color='#6a4c93', width=1)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=forecast_df['Date'], y=forecast_df['Forecast'], name='Forecast',
                          line=dict(color='#ff595e', width=2)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=forecast_df['Date'], y=forecast_df['Upper'], name='Upper 80%',
                          line=dict(color='#ff595e', dash='dot', width=0.5), showlegend=False))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=forecast_df['Date'], y=forecast_df['Lower'], name='80% CI',
                          line=dict(color='#ff595e', dash='dot', width=0.5),
                          fill='tonexty', fillcolor='rgba(255, 89, 94, 0.15)'))

fig.update_layout(height=450, template='plotly_white',
                  title='90-Day Sales Forecast with 80% Confidence Band',
                  yaxis_title='Sales (€)', xaxis_title='')
fig.show()




                                                


Figure 3: Historical sales and 90-day forecast

avg_daily = forecast_df['Forecast'].mean()
peak_day = forecast_df.loc[forecast_df['Forecast'].idxmax(), 'Date']
peak_value = forecast_df['Forecast'].max()

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'Metric': ['Total 90-day forecast', 'Average daily sales', 'Peak day', 'Peak value'],
    'Value': [f'€{total_forecast:,.0f}',

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
What this tells the business






ImportantActionable insights




Staff up for weekends — the Saturday/Sunday lift is consistent enough to plan for.
The forecast trend is upward, reflecting the underlying growth — capacity planning should reflect that, not flat last-year numbers.
The 80% confidence band is tight enough to give stock planners a usable range. Revisit in 30 days with actuals.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
What I learned

Decomposition before forecasting is non-negotiable. Looking at trend/season/residual separately showed the pattern was stable and the model could be simple.
A simple model that you understand beats a complex one you don’t. I could have reached for Prophet or ARIMA, but a moving-average + seasonal map is transparent, cheap to retrain, and adequately accurate for a 90-day horizon.
Confidence bands matter more than point estimates — decision-makers need to know the uncertainty, not a pretend-precise single line.

title: Reflection
text:
Note



This page is my honest reflection on the skills I picked up building this ePortfolio and what I want to carry forward.

title: Reflection
text:
Starting point
When I started this module I had a clear undergraduate foundation in IT and a reasonable grasp of Python from coursework, but I had never built a website from scratch, never deployed anything to the public internet, and never used Git beyond the occasional git clone. By the end of this module, I had to combine all three to produce this site. That gap — between knowing things in isolation and shipping them together — turned out to be the most valuable part of the learning.

title: Reflection
text:
Git and version control
The thing that surprised me most about Git was how quickly it stopped feeling like a chore. My first commits were cautious — small, nervous pushes with messages like “update” and “fix”. Within a day I was committing on purpose, writing messages that actually described why I made a change, not just what I changed. That shift mattered.
What clicked:

Small commits are better than big ones. If something breaks, you can walk back one step.
.gitignore is not optional. I accidentally committed a .DS_Store file early on and it taught me to set that up from the start.
The GitHub Pages deploy loop is fast. Commit → push → 30 seconds → live.1 That tight feedback loop made me more willing to experiment.

What I’d still like to learn: branching and merge conflicts. I worked on main the whole time because it was a solo project, but I know team workflows require feature branches, pull requests, and reviews.

title: Reflection
text:
Quarto
Quarto was new to me. I picked it because the brief required it, but I ended up genuinely liking it. The idea of writing in Markdown, dropping in live Python code, and getting a polished site out the other end feels like the right abstraction for the kind of data work I want to do.
What I built comfort with:

YAML frontmatter to control page behaviour (About templates, listing pages, code folding)
Project-wide configuration through _quarto.yml — navbar, footer, theme, SCSS
The {python} code chunk and its options (fig-cap, code-fold, echo)
Callout blocks, grids, and rich Markdown features

What I struggled with: the first time my _quarto.yml had a tiny indentation error, the whole render broke with a cryptic message. I learned to render after every significant change rather than stacking up edits blindly.

title: Reflection
text:
Python for analytics
I’d used Python before, but mostly in isolated notebooks for class exercises. Building the two project pages — Customer Segmentation with RFM and Sales Forecasting — pushed me to think about Python as a tool for communicating analysis, not just running it.
Writing analyses for an audience that isn’t the grader changed how I wrote code:

I started naming variables for readers, not for myself
I split code into small blocks with narrative between them
I picked visualisations for what they showed, not for what was easy to plot
I learned to use Plotly for interactivity, where a static matplotlib chart would have shortened the file but lost the reader

title: Reflection
section: Web design as a learning experience
text:
Web design as a learning experience
I did not expect to spend as much time thinking about design as I did. Choosing a theme, picking fonts, tuning a colour palette — these weren’t decisions I’d ever made consciously before. I came out with a much better appreciation for why designers care about hierarchy, whitespace, and typography.
The custom styles.scss file was where I learned the most. Bootswatch gives you a competent starting point; Sass variables give you real control. Changing one $primary variable and watching every link, button, and navbar element shift colour was weirdly satisfying.

title: Reflection
text:
Biggest mistakes (and lessons)






WarningLessons from mistakes I actually made




404 panic. Early on my site returned 404 for about 15 minutes and I thought I’d broken something fundamental. It was just GitHub Pages propagation — patience is part of the workflow.
YAML frontmatter. I accidentally pasted content without the --- frontmatter delimiters and the landing page rendered as plain Markdown. Lesson: always check the top three lines.
Rendering before pushing. A few times I pushed without rendering and wondered why the live site hadn’t updated. The docs/ folder is what gets served — if you don’t render, you push stale HTML.

title: Reflection
text:
Skills I’m taking forward
Beyond this module, this is the kit I now have:

I can ship. I can go from “blank folder” to “live website with interactive analysis” in a day.
I can version. Every project I build from now on will live in Git from the first commit.
I can communicate. Technical writing, charts-as-argument, and structured narrative are skills I’ll use in every analyst role I apply for.
I can iterate. The render → commit → push → refresh loop is a pattern I can apply to any deliverable, not just websites.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text: Not every customer is equally valuable — and not every customer should get the same marketing treatment. How can we segment a customer base into meaningful groups using only three simple signals: Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value?

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text: Not every customer is equally valuable — and not every customer should get the same marketing treatment. How can we segment a customer base into meaningful groups using only three simple signals: Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value?

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
The Approach
RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) is a classic marketing framework.1 I combine it with K-Means clustering to identify natural customer segments without hand-picking thresholds.
The composite RFM score weights each standardised dimension equally:
\[\text{RFM Score} = w_R \cdot \tilde{R} + w_F \cdot \tilde{F} + w_M \cdot \tilde{M}\]
where \(\tilde{R}\), \(\tilde{F}\), and \(\tilde{M}\) are the standardised Recency, Frequency, and Monetary values, and \(w_R + w_F + w_M = 1\). In this project all weights are set to \(\frac{1}{3}\), but they can be tuned to reflect business priorities.






Note



Data in this project is synthetic — generated to simulate realistic retail patterns. The methodology is what matters; the same pipeline runs on real transaction data without changes.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Step 1 — Generate the data


Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

np.random.seed(42)

n_customers = 1000
today = datetime(2026, 4, 15)

# Simulate customer behaviour with three archetypes mixed in
customer_ids = range(1, n_customers + 1)
recency = np.concatenate([
    np.random.randint(1, 30, 300),     # active
    np.random.randint(30, 120, 500),   # moderate
    np.random.randint(120, 365, 200)   # lapsed
])
frequency = np.concatenate([
    np.random.randint(10, 50, 300),
    np.random.randint(3, 10, 500),
    np.random.randint(1, 3, 200)
])
monetary = np.concatenate([
    np.random.uniform(500, 5000, 300),
    np.random.uniform(100, 500, 500),
    np.random.uniform(10, 100, 200)
]).round(2)

rfm = pd.DataFrame({
    'CustomerID': customer_ids,
    'Recency': recency,
    'Frequency': frequency,
    'Monetary': monetary
})

Figure 1: Distribution of Recency, Frequency, and Monetary values




The three features are heavily right-skewed — a handful of customers dominate frequency and spend. This is exactly what we’d expect in retail and motivates scaling before clustering.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Step 3 — Cluster with K-Means


Code
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Scale features (K-Means is distance-based, so scale matters)
scaler = StandardScaler()
rfm_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(rfm[['Recency', 'Frequency', 'Monetary']])

# Fit K-Means with 4 clusters
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=42, n_init=10)
rfm['Cluster'] = kmeans.fit_predict(rfm_scaled)

# Profile each cluster
cluster_profile = rfm.groupby('Cluster').agg(
    Count=('CustomerID', 'count'),
    AvgRecency=('Recency', 'mean'),
    AvgFrequency=('Frequency', 'mean'),
    AvgMonetary=('Monetary', 'mean')
).round(1)

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Step 4 — Name the segments
Based on the cluster profile, I can assign meaningful labels:


Code
segment_names = {
    rfm.groupby('Cluster')['Monetary'].mean().idxmax(): '🌟 Champions',
    rfm.groupby('Cluster')['Recency'].mean().idxmax(): '💤 At Risk',
    rfm.groupby('Cluster')['Frequency'].mean().idxmin(): '🆕 New / Occasional',
}
# Fill in the remaining cluster
remaining = set(rfm['Cluster'].unique()) - set(segment_names.keys())
for c in remaining:
    segment_names[c] = '👥 Loyal Regulars'

rfm['Segment'] = rfm['Cluster'].map(segment_names)

title: 3XM Data Analytics Project
text: The primary objective of this project is to build a supervised ML model that predicts real revenue based on sales data from 2023-present. The project explores features such as product type, country, and shipping method, and how these features impact real revenue. The goal is to utilise this model to enhance operational decision making and marketing strategies by analysing the impact of features on real revenue.

title: 3XM Data Analytics Project
text:
Data Preparation & Cleaning
The raw dataset required several preprocessing steps before modelling:

Voucher column converted to a binary indicator (voucher_used: 1 if a voucher was applied, 0 otherwise)
Country names standardised — encoding issues corrected (e.g. '√É‚Äìsterreich' → 'Austria', 'Sverige' → 'Sweden') and UK regions unified under 'United Kingdom'
Date features engineered into order_month, order_quarter, order_dayofweek, and order_year
Irrelevant columns dropped: order_id, photographer_id, voucher, activation_date, payment_method, payment_date, date
Dummy variable encoding applied to currency and country_clean

# Standardise country names
country_name = {
    'USA': 'United States',
    'Nederland': 'Netherlands',
    'Sverige': 'Sweden',
    'England': 'United Kingdom',
    'Scotland': 'United Kingdom',
    'Wales': 'United Kingdom',
    'Northern Ireland': 'United Kingdom'
}
df['country_clean'] = df['country'].replace(country_name)

# Engineer date features
df['order_month']     = df['date'].dt.month
df['order_quarter']   = df['date'].dt.quarter
df['order_dayofweek'] = df['date'].dt.dayofweek
df['order_year']      = df['date'].dt.year

title: 3XM Data Analytics Project
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
IQR-based outlier detection was applied to the real_revenue target variable to understand its distribution. A correlation check revealed that total (order total before deductions) was extremely highly correlated with real_revenue (~0.999), raising a data leakage concern.
Q1 = df['real_revenue'].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = df['real_revenue'].quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1

lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
outliers = df[(df['real_revenue'] < lower_bound) | (df['real_revenue'] > upper_bound)]
print("Number of outliers:", len(outliers))

# Correlation check
np.corrcoef(df['real_revenue'], df['total'])

title: 3XM Data Analytics Project
text:
Random Forest Models
Two separate Random Forest Regressors were trained to test the effect of data leakage:

Model 1 — includes the total column (high correlation with target)
Model 2 — excludes total to evaluate the genuine predictive power of remaining features

Both models used 300 trees, max_features=None, and 5-fold cross-validation.
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=None, random_state=42)
rf.fit(train_x, train_y)
y_pred = rf.predict(test_x)

cv_r2   = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring='r2')
cv_rmse = np.sqrt(-cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg_mean_squared_error'))
cv_mae  = -cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error')

title: 3XM Data Analytics Project
text:
Conclusion
This project highlights the critical importance of data leakage prevention in ML pipelines. Including a near-perfectly correlated feature (total) creates an artificially high-performing model that would fail in production. The clean pipeline — without total — provides a realistic and deployable revenue prediction model, exported as clean_dataset.csv for further business use.
Key takeaways:

Always inspect feature correlations with the target before modelling
Cross-validation gives a more honest performance estimate than a single train/test split
Feature engineering from dates (month, quarter) adds genuine predictive signal

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text: Accurate sales forecasting is essential for inventory management, staffing, and revenue planning. This project applies classical time series decomposition and moving-average smoothing to forecast 90 days of retail sales, with results presented in an interactive Plotly dashboard accessible to non-technical stakeholders.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text: Accurate sales forecasting is essential for inventory management, staffing, and revenue planning. This project applies classical time series decomposition and moving-average smoothing to forecast 90 days of retail sales, with results presented in an interactive Plotly dashboard accessible to non-technical stakeholders.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Data & Approach
The dataset contains 2 years of daily retail sales. Before modelling, stationarity was checked using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test, and strong weekly seasonality (peaking Fridays/Saturdays) was confirmed visually.
A multiplicative decomposition was chosen over additive because seasonal amplitude grew proportionally with the trend — a common pattern in growing retail businesses.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Time Series Decomposition
The sales series was decomposed into three components using statsmodels:
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

result = seasonal_decompose(
    sales_series,
    model='multiplicative',
    period=7           # weekly seasonality
)

trend    = result.trend
seasonal = result.seasonal
residual = result.resid
Decomposing first allows us to forecast the trend and seasonal components separately, then recombine them — giving more accurate and interpretable results than black-box methods.

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Forecasting Method
A 28-day rolling moving average was applied to the trend component to smooth noise and project forward. The seasonal component (weekly pattern) was layered back in multiplicatively to produce the final 90-day forecast.
Confidence intervals were estimated from the standard deviation of residuals, providing ±1 and ±2 standard deviation bands.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 28-day MA on trend
trend_ma = trend.rolling(window=28, center=True).mean()

# Project trend forward (linear extrapolation of last 30 days)
trend_slope = np.polyfit(range(30), trend_ma.dropna().values[-30:], 1)
trend_forecast = np.polyval(trend_slope, range(1, 91))

# Layer back seasonal component (average seasonal pattern)
seasonal_pattern = seasonal[-7:].values  # last full weekly cycle
seasonal_forecast = np.tile(seasonal_pattern, 13)[:90]

# Final forecast = trend × seasonal
forecast = trend_forecast * seasonal_forecast

# Confidence intervals from residual std
resid_std = residual.std()
upper_1 = forecast * (1 + resid_std)
lower_1 = forecast * (1 - resid_std)

title: Sales Forecasting Dashboard
text:
Interactive Plotly Dashboard
The dashboard includes four panels:

Historical sales with 7-day and 28-day MA overlays

Seasonal pattern — isolated weekly cycle
Trend-only view for long-term direction

import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=['Historical + MA', '90-Day Forecast',
                    'Weekly Seasonality', 'Trend Component'])

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dates, y=sales, name='Actual', line=dict(color='#3a6447')), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=forecast_dates, y=forecast, name='Forecast',

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
This project investigates two paradigms of NLP for business sentiment analysis:

Fine-tuned BERT — a discriminative transformer model trained on labelled data
Llama 3.1 — a large generative model evaluated with zero-shot and few-shot prompting

The Rotten Tomatoes movie review dataset provides a binary classification task (positive / negative), serving as a realistic business proxy for customer feedback analysis.

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
This project investigates two paradigms of NLP for business sentiment analysis:

Fine-tuned BERT — a discriminative transformer model trained on labelled data
Llama 3.1 — a large generative model evaluated with zero-shot and few-shot prompting

The Rotten Tomatoes movie review dataset provides a binary classification task (positive / negative), serving as a realistic business proxy for customer feedback analysis.

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
Motivation
Businesses increasingly rely on sentiment analysis to understand customer feedback at scale. Two leading approaches have emerged:

Fine-tuning a pre-trained model like BERT requires labelled training data but achieves high accuracy on the target domain
Prompting a generative model like Llama 3.1 requires no labelled data, enabling rapid deployment in low-resource settings

This project rigorously compares both approaches on identical data.

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
BERT Fine-Tuning
bert-base-uncased was fine-tuned using Hugging Face Transformers. A classification head was added on top of the [CLS] token representation. Training used AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule for 3 epochs, batch size 16.
from transformers import BertForSequenceClassification, BertTokenizer
from torch.optim import AdamW
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import get_cosine_schedule_with_warmup

tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    'bert-base-uncased', num_labels=2
)

optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-5)
scheduler = get_cosine_schedule_with_warmup(
    optimizer, num_warmup_steps=100, num_training_steps=len(train_loader)*3
)

# Training loop — 3 epochs, batch size 16
for epoch in range(3):
    model.train()
    for batch in train_loader:
        outputs = model(**batch)
        loss = outputs.loss
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        scheduler.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
Llama 3.1 Prompting
Llama 3.1 was evaluated in two settings:

Zero-shot — model receives only the review text and is asked to classify
Few-shot — model receives 3 labelled examples before classifying the target review

# Few-shot prompt template
def build_prompt(review, examples):
    prompt = "Classify each movie review as positive or negative.\n\n"
    for ex_review, ex_label in examples:
        prompt += f"Review: {ex_review}\nSentiment: {ex_label}\n\n"
    prompt += f"Review: {review}\nSentiment:"
    return prompt

Fine-tuned BERT achieved the highest accuracy, benefiting from task-specific training. Llama 3.1 few-shot prompting performed competitively with no labelled training data. Zero-shot Llama showed more inconsistency on nuanced or sarcastic reviews.

title: BERT vs. Generative AI for Business Applications: A Sentiment Analysis Comparison Using Rotten Tomatoes Reviews
text:
Conclusion
Fine-tuned BERT remains the gold standard for classification when labelled data is available. However, generative models like Llama 3.1 offer a compelling alternative for rapid prototyping or low-resource settings where annotation is costly.
Business implications:

If labelled data exists → fine-tune BERT for maximum accuracy
If speed-to-deployment matters → few-shot Llama achieves ~83% with no annotation cost
Zero-shot is viable for quick experiments but not production-grade sentiment pipelines

The choice ultimately depends on business constraints around labelling budget vs. time-to-deployment vs. accuracy requirements.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text: Recency-Frequency-Monetary (RFM) analysis is a proven marketing framework for understanding customer behaviour. This project applies RFM scoring and K-Means clustering to segment 1,000 synthetic retail customers into meaningful groups that can directly inform targeted marketing strategies.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text: Recency-Frequency-Monetary (RFM) analysis is a proven marketing framework for understanding customer behaviour. This project applies RFM scoring and K-Means clustering to segment 1,000 synthetic retail customers into meaningful groups that can directly inform targeted marketing strategies.

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
RFM Feature Engineering
Three features were calculated per customer from transaction history:

Recency — days since the customer’s last purchase (lower = more recent = better)
Frequency — number of purchases within the analysis period
Monetary — total spend over the period

Each raw value was then scaled using StandardScaler before clustering to prevent any single dimension from dominating.
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

snapshot_date = pd.Timestamp('2026-04-01')

# Calculate RFM features per customer
rfm = df.groupby('customer_id').agg(
    Recency   = ('order_date', lambda x: (snapshot_date - x.max()).days),
    Frequency = ('order_id',   'count'),
    Monetary  = ('revenue',    'sum')
).reset_index()

# Scale features
scaler = StandardScaler()
rfm_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(rfm[['Recency', 'Frequency', 'Monetary']])

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Selecting the Optimal K
The Elbow Method (inertia vs K) and Silhouette Scores were both used to select the number of clusters. K=4 was chosen — it produced the clearest elbow and the highest silhouette score, while remaining interpretable for business stakeholders.
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

inertias, silhouettes = [], []
for k in range(2, 11):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    labels = km.fit_predict(rfm_scaled)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(rfm_scaled, labels))

# K=4 selected based on elbow + silhouette
km_final = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=42, n_init=10)
rfm['Cluster'] = km_final.fit_predict(rfm_scaled)

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Marketing Strategies by Segment
Champions (22%) — Recent, frequent, high-spend buyers. These are your best customers.

Reward with loyalty programmes or early access to new products
Ask for reviews and referrals

Loyal Customers (31%) — Regular buyers with moderate spend. High potential.

Upsell to premium products or bundles
Cross-sell complementary categories

At-Risk (28%) — Previously active customers who haven’t purchased recently.

Send targeted re-engagement emails with personalised offers
Highlight new arrivals relevant to their purchase history

Lost Customers (19%) — Low recency, low frequency, low spend. Mostly churned.

Win-back campaign with a compelling discount
If no response after 2 attempts, discontinue spend on this segment

title: Customer Segmentation with RFM Analysis
text:
Conclusion
RFM-based K-Means clustering provides a practical, interpretable framework for customer segmentation that any marketing team can act on. The four identified segments enable efficient budget allocation — concentrating retention spend on Champions and Loyal Customers while deploying re-engagement tactics for At-Risk customers.
Key learnings:

Scaling features before clustering is essential — unscaled RFM produces misleading segments
Combining Elbow + Silhouette gives more confidence in K selection than either alone
Always interpret cluster centroids in the original (unscaled) space for business communication


Tools: Python, Scikit-learn, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn
